name: Asel
title: Descendant of King Saul in the tribe of Benjamin
summary: Asel was a Benjaminite from Saul's royal lineage, the son of Elasa and brother of Esek. His name appears in the detailed genealogies in 1 Chronicles, where he is mentioned as the father of six sons: Asrikam, Bokru, Ismael, Searja, Obadja, and Hanan. The genealogy appears twice – in chapter 8 and chapter 9 – with the latter placing the family line in the context of the return from the Babylonian exile and settlement in Jerusalem. Asel's place in the register shows that the royal line from Benjamin was carefully preserved over many generations, even long after Saul's kingdom had fallen. In this way, his position in the genealogy serves as a link between the pre-exilic monarchy and the post-exilic community.
roles: Ancestor in the tribe of Benjamin

keyEvents.title: Asel in Saul's Genealogy
keyEvents.description: Asel is mentioned as the son of Elasa in the genealogy of Saul's descendants through the Jonathan line in the tribe of Benjamin.

keyEvents.title: Asel's Six Sons
keyEvents.description: Asel had six sons, all named: Azrikam, Bokeru, Ishmael, Shearja, Obadiah, and Hanan. The detailed listing highlights his role as a patriarch and the continuation of the royal lineage.

keyEvents.title: Descendants of Asel's Brother Esek – Skilled Archers
keyEvents.description: Asel's brother Esek had a son named Ulam, whose descendants were skilled archers with 150 sons and grandsons. This testifies to the enduring military strength in the tribe of Benjamin.

keyEvents.title: Genealogy Repeated in Connection with Settlement in Jerusalem
keyEvents.description: Asel's genealogy is repeated in 1 Chronicles chapter 9, where it is linked to the list of those who settled in Jerusalem after returning from the Babylonian exile. The repetition gives the genealogy an expanded function as legitimization of the tribe's continued presence.

versions.summary: Asel (Hebrew: Atsel) was a descendant of King Saul through the Jonathan line in the tribe of Benjamin. He is mentioned in the genealogies in 1 Chronicles as the son of Elasa and father of six sons. His lineage shows that Saul's descendants continued to hold some significance in Israel.
versions.title: Descendant of King Saul
versions.reason: [major] 1 Chr 8:39-40 concerns the sons and descendants of Ulam, not Azel. Verse 39 introduces Ulam (son of Eshek/Eshak, brother of Azel), and verse 40 states that Ulam's sons were skilled archers with 150 sons and grandsons. This is incorrectly attributed to Azel.; [major] 1 Chr 8:39-40 refers to the descendants of Ulam (who was a brother or relative of Azel), not directly to Azel himself. This event should either be removed or corrected.; [minor] The title 'patriarch' is somewhat misleading for Azel. He is primarily a genealogical figure/ancestor in a lineage, not a patriarch in the traditional biblical sense (like Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob). 'Ancestor' or 'genealogical link' would be more precise.; [minor] The dating 'c. 900–800 BC' is highly uncertain. Azel is one of many generations between Jonathan and the post-exilic period. Depending on the number of generations, he may have lived earlier or later. It might be better to indicate this with broader uncertainty.; [minor] The children's names (such as 'Bokru', 'Ishmael', 'Seariah', 'Obadiah', 'Hanan') could be confused with other biblical figures bearing the same names. Otherwise, the names appear correct based on 1 Chr 8:38.; [minor] The title is clear but could have been more specific, for example, 'Descendant of King Saul through the line of Jonathan'.

versions.title: Descendant of King Saul through the Jonathan Line
versions.reason: [minor] The summary is very similar to version 1 (begins with the same wording 'Asel (Hebrew: Atsel) was a descendant of King Saul through the Jonathan line in the tribe of Benjamin'). It should be rephrased to distinguish itself more clearly from the previous version.; [major] The event concerning Ulam's descendants actually refers to the descendants of Asel's brother Esek, but the text says 'Asel's brother (or relative) Esek's son Ulam'. According to 1 Chr 8:39, Esek is Asel's brother, and Ulam is Esek's son. The wording is unclear and should be clarified. Furthermore, this event does not directly concern Asel himself, but rather the descendants of his brother.; [minor] This event primarily concerns Asel's brother Esek and his descendants, not Asel directly. It may still be retained as context, but it should be made clearer.; [minor] The lifespan 'approx. 900–800 BC' is uncertain. Depending on how many generations are counted from Saul (approx. 1050–1010 BC) through the Jonathan line to Asel, the dating may vary. It is reasonable but uncertain and should be clearly marked as estimated.; [minor] The era 'divided-kingdom' is reasonable given the assumed lifespan, but the genealogies were compiled in the post-exilic period. The person himself likely lived during the divided kingdom period, so this is acceptable.; [minor] The footnote about Ulam and archers refers to Judg 20:16 regarding sling throwers, but the biblical parallel is not entirely precise – Judg 20:16 concerns left-handed sling throwers, while Ulam's descendants were archers. Nevertheless, both illustrate Benjamin's military reputation.

versions.summary: Azel belonged to the royal lineage from Saul and Jonathan in the tribe of Benjamin, and was the son of Elasa. In the genealogies in 1 Chronicles he is mentioned as the father of six named sons: Azrikam, Bokeru, Ishmael, Shearja, Obadiah, and Hanan. His genealogy is repeated in two chapters (1 Chr 8 and 9), which reflects the book of Chronicles' desire to document the tribe's continuity, especially concerning those who returned to Jerusalem after the Babylonian exile. Through Azel's lineage it is shown that the royal line from Benjamin continued long after Saul's kingdom had ended.

It is relevant context, but could have been formulated more clearly as contextual information rather than a key event for Azel.; [minor] This event overlaps significantly with keyEvents[0] and keyEvents[3]. It is more of a summary or theological reflection than a distinct event. Consider merging it with the repetition in chapter 9.; [minor] The summary is good, but since this is the third version, it should be tightened further. The phrasing 'not least in connection with those who returned' is somewhat vague. This could be clarified somewhat more and made more distinct from earlier versions.; [minor] In some translations the brother's name is 'Esek', while others show variations. Check that 'esek' is the correct ID – in 1 Chr 8:39 he is named Esek (Hebrew: עֵשֶׁק). The ID 'esek' appears correct.; [minor] The dating 'c. 900–800 BC' is highly uncertain. Given that Azel lived many generations after Saul (c. 1050–1010 BC) and there are approximately 8–9 generations between Jonathan and Azel, the dating may be reasonable, but it remains highly speculative. The label '(uncertain)' is appropriate.

footnotes.text: The name Asel (Hebrew: אָצֵל, 'atsel) may mean 'noble' or 'reserved/set apart'. Some scholars link it to the Hebrew root meaning 'to set aside' or 'to reserve', which could suggest a person chosen or set apart for a task.

The genealogies in 1 Chronicles 8–9 were likely compiled in the post-exilic period to document tribal origins and legitimize family affiliations after the return from Babylon. The detailed preservation of Saul's lineage shows that the tribe of Benjamin still held significance in the Jewish community after the exile.

The repetition of Asel's genealogy in both 1 Chronicles 8 and 9 is an example of Chronicles' literary technique of double tradition. Chapter 9 specifically links the genealogies to those who settled in Jerusalem after the Babylonian exile, giving the register a new function beyond pure genealogy.

According to 1 Chron 8:40, Asel's brother Ezer's son Ulam had descendants who were skilled archers, with 150 sons and grandsons. The tribe of Benjamin was known for its military prowess, which is also reflected in Judg 20:16, where Benjaminites are described as exceptionally accurate warriors.

The tribe of Benjamin held a unique place in Israel's history. Despite being nearly wiped out in the civil war described in the Book of Judges (chaps. 19–21), it survived and produced Israel's first king, Saul. The fact that Chronicles preserves detailed genealogies from this tribe underscores its enduring significance.

In rabbinic tradition, detailed genealogies were not only regarded as historical documents but also as expressions of God's faithfulness to His people. The preservation of Saul's lineage through Asel and his sons illustrates that even after the kingdom was taken away from Saul's house, the family was still honored and kept alive in the collective memory of the people.
